title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
Charging from zero
Starting from 0 V toward a supply \(V_s\):
\[
V(t) = V_s \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)
\]
Discharging back toward 0 V from \(V_s\) follows the mirror image, \(V(t) = V_s e^{-t/\tau}\).

title: Ohm’s law and power
text: The relationship every other circuit identity gets built on top of.

title: Ohm’s law and power
text:
The law
For a resistor, voltage and current are proportional:
\[
V = IR
\]
Power dissipated follows from \(P = VI\), substituted with Ohm’s law to give two more useful forms:
\[
P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
\]
The \(I^2R\) form is the one that matters for sizing: double the current through a fixed resistance and dissipation quadruples, not doubles — a common reason parts run hotter than expected after a “small” current increase.

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Loaded divider
Once something draws current from the output node — an ADC input, another circuit — that load resistor \(R_L\) sits in parallel with \(R_2\), and the divider ratio changes:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2 \| R_L}{R_1 + (R_2 \| R_L)}, \qquad R_2 \| R_L = \frac{R_2 R_L}{R_2 + R_L}
\]
This is why a divider that measures correctly open-circuit can read low once connected to a real load — the rule of thumb is to keep \(R_L \gg R_2\), typically 10× or more.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text: A quick derivation of solenoid inductance from first principles, then the practical correction engineers actually use, with a calculator to try real turn counts and dimensions.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
The ideal case
Treating the coil as infinitely long, Ampere’s law gives a uniform field inside: \(B = \mu_0 n I\), where \(n = N / l\) is turns per unit length. Flux linkage through all \(N\) turns gives:
\[
L_{ideal} = \mu_0 N^2 \frac{\pi r^2}{l}
\]
This overestimates inductance for any real, finite coil — it ignores fringing at the ends.



Fig. 1 — field concentrated inside the winding, with fringing paths returning outside.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
Wheeler’s correction
For a real single-layer coil where length isn’t much greater than radius, Wheeler’s 1928 approximation is the standard practical formula (\(r\), \(l\) in inches, result in \(\mu H\)):
\[
L_{\mu H} \approx \frac{r^2 N^2}{9r + 10l}
\]
Valid roughly for \(l > 0.4r\). Below that, it undercorrects and a full Nagaoka-coefficient treatment is needed.



Fig. 2 — field strength rising with current, fringing appearing at the ends.

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Parallel
Resistors in parallel share the same voltage, and their currents add, giving a reciprocal sum:
\[
\frac{1}{R_{parallel}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}
\]
The parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor — adding a path for current can only make it easier for current to flow.

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
Series RLC magnitude
For R, L, and C in series, the reactances subtract (they’re 180° apart) before combining with resistance:
\[
|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}
\]
This hits a minimum, \(|Z| = R\), at the resonant frequency where \(X_L = X_C\).
